title: N-Queens
corePattern: Backtracking with Constraint Pruning - Row-by-Row Placement with Column and Diagonal Conflict Elimination
interviewTips: Clarify: return all distinct board configurations as List[List[str]] with 'Q' and '.' - ask if n=0 should return [] or [[]] (LeetCode returns []).
Trade-off: O(1) safety check via hash sets / bitmask vs O(n) board scan - explain how pruning reduces N^N naive search to roughly N! nodes.
Edge-case tip: n=2 and n=3 have zero solutions, n=1 has one solution [['Q']]; mention bitmask overflow for n>32 in Java/C++ int and use long if needed.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Backtracking with O(N) Safety Scan
approaches.intuition: Place one queen per row to automatically satisfy row constraint. For row r try every column c, scan upward column and both upper diagonals to verify no attack, place and recurse to r+1, then undo (backtrack). If r==n we found a valid board.
approaches.theory: N-Queens is exact-cover / constraint satisfaction. By fixing row order we reduce search from N^(N^2) to N^N, and safety pruning further cuts to permutation-like search. Correctness by induction: invariant is first r rows are pairwise non-attacking; isSafe ensures extension preserves invariant; enumeration of all c ensures completeness.

timeComplexity.explanation: Search tree has at most N! / pruned nodes (permutations of columns). Each isSafe scans column + 2 diagonals up to O(N). Copying board on solution costs O(N^2) amortized over few solutions.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Board O(N^2) plus recursion depth O(N). Output storage not counted except board; storing all solutions takes O(S * N^2) where S is number of solutions.

steps: row 0: try c=0 -> place Q at (0,0), recurse
row 1: c=0,1 attacked, c=2 safe -> place (1,2), recurse
row 2: all c=0..3 attacked -> backtrack, row1 try c=3 -> place (1,3)
row 2: c=1 safe -> place (2,1), row3: no safe cell -> backtrack
row 0: try c=1 -> place (0,1), leads to solution [(0,1),(1,3),(2,0),(3,2)] and [(0,2),(1,0),(2,3),(3,1)] after full search

edgeCases: n=2 and n=3 return [] - no placement possible, must still explore and backtrack correctly
n=0 (if tested) return [] - avoid (1<<n)-1 edge or empty board copy errors

approaches.name: Approach 2: Backtracking with Bitmask O(1) Conflict Check
approaches.intuition: Encode attacked columns and two diagonals as bitmasks. For current row, available = allOnes & ~(cols | d1 | d2). Each 1-bit is a safe column. Pick lowest set bit, place queen, update masks for next row by shifting diagonals left/right, recurse. Clearing bit iterates only over safe spots.
approaches.theory: Column index c maps to bit 1<<c. diag1 (r+c constant, \) shifts left each row, diag2 (r-c constant, /) shifts right each row because diagonal attack moves by one column per row. available computation is exact set of non-attacked columns - proof by invariant that cols/d1/d2 contain all attacks from previous rows. Extracting bit with x & -x and iterating gives optimal branching without scanning board.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int):
        res = []
        board = [['.' for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n)]
        def backtrack(row, cols, d1, d2):
            if row == n:
                res.append([''.join(r) for r in board])
                return
            avail = ((1 << n) - 1) & ~(cols | d1 | d2)
            while avail:
                bit = avail & -avail
                col = bit.bit_length() - 1
                board[row][col] = 'Q'
                backtrack(row + 1, cols | bit, (d1 | bit) << 1, (d2 | bit) >> 1)
                board[row][col] = '.'
                avail &= avail - 1
        backtrack(0, 0, 0, 0)
        return res

timeComplexity.explanation: Same search nodes as backtracking but safety check is O(1) bit operations and loop iterates only over valid columns, not all N. Still exponential - N-Queens counting is #P-complete, cannot be polynomial.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Three integer masks + recursion depth O(N) plus board O(N^2) for construction. Masks replace O(N) boolean arrays/sets, minimal extra memory.

steps: row0: cols=0,d1=0,d2=0, avail=1111, pick bit0001 col0 -> recurse with cols=0001,d1=0010,d2=0000
row1: avail=1111 & ~0011 =1100 (col2,3 only) -> pick col2, update masks
row2: avail computed =0000 -> dead end, backtrack and pick col3
row0 pick col1 -> path leads to avail non-empty each row -> record 2 full solutions

edgeCases: n=1: avail=1, bit=1, col=0 -> single solution
n=2,3: bit iteration quickly empties, returns [] without error
n>=31 overflow of (1<<n) in 32-bit int - LeetCode n<=9 so safe; for larger n use long / Python int
